title: Trust is retreating toward familiar circles as economic anxiety, geopolitical tension, and technological disruption widen social distance
source_unit: Edelman Trust Institute, 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer
geography: Published global trust survey covering 28 countries, with cross-country and socioeconomic comparisons

denominator.unit: online survey respondents across 28 countries in the published Trust Barometer research frame

insular_mindset.unit: percent unwilling or hesitant to trust someone with different values, facts, problem-solving approaches, or cultural background

insularity_pattern.value: people are narrowing trust toward smaller, familiar circles amid economic anxiety, geopolitical tension, and technological disruption

social_consequence.value: insularity can hinder economic and societal progress by making difference an obstacle to collaboration

observations.method: Edelman Trust Institute online interviews conducted October 25-November 16, 2025, summarized at global and country levels.
observations.uncertainty: This is a private survey's published aggregate result, not a probability-sample estimate of every population; question wording, fieldwork, weighting, and cultural interpretation matter.
observations.subgroup: People across 28 countries, socioeconomic groups, cultural backgrounds, institutions, employers, media users, and communities experiencing polarization.
observations.counterinterpretation: Familiar networks can provide safety, solidarity, and practical trust during shocks; skepticism toward difference may reflect perceived institutional failure rather than simple intolerance.

denominator.unit: global survey comparison of expectations for the next generation

next_generation_better_off.unit: percent who believe the next generation will be better off

largest_declines.value: India and China each recorded a 13-point decline over the prior year in the published comparison

optimism_channel.value: economic anxiety, technology disruption, and geopolitical tension shape expectations about social mobility and collective progress

observations.method: Edelman global survey comparison of expectations across countries and over time.
observations.uncertainty: Optimism is an attitudinal indicator and does not measure actual intergenerational mobility, income, employment, or public-service outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Young people, parents, workers, low-income households, emerging economies, and people judging institutional and economic trajectories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low optimism can coexist with local agency, cultural vitality, or high expectations for reform; survey sentiment can shift faster than structural conditions.

observations.period: 2026; social-media trust brokering and commercial credibility

denominator.unit: published comparison among people who trust at least one relevant social-media influencer

food_lifestyle_influencer.unit: percent among the 48 percent who trust a food or lifestyle influencer who would consider or trust a company vouched for by that influencer

financial_influencer.unit: percent among the 44 percent who trust a financial influencer who would consider or trust a company vouched for by that influencer

trust_channel.value: trusted intermediaries can open closed doors between people and institutions or brands they currently distrust

observations.method: Edelman published aggregate cross-tabulation of influencer trust and willingness to trust a vouched-for company.
observations.uncertainty: These are conditional associations, not causal endorsement effects, purchase outcomes, or evidence that influencers are reliable brokers of public information.
observations.subgroup: Social-media users, consumers, influencers, brands, financial-service users, and people with low trust in formal institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trusted intermediaries can help translate unfamiliar institutions, but sponsorship, commercial incentives, misinformation, and personalization can also deepen manipulation or fragmentation.

denominator.unit: global high-income and low-income trust comparison over time

income_trust_gap.value: the global trust gap between high- and low-income groups has more than doubled since 2012

high_low_pattern.value: trust has risen among high earners while stagnating or lagging among low-income groups

us_gap.unit: percentage-point income-based trust gap reported for the United States

observations.method: Edelman longitudinal aggregate comparison of trust by income group and country.
observations.uncertainty: The published gap does not identify which institutions or experiences cause divergence, and income categories and survey modes may not be directly comparable across countries and years.
observations.subgroup: High- and low-income groups, workers, consumers, institutions, employers, governments, and communities experiencing unequal economic security.
observations.counterinterpretation: Trust gaps may narrow when material security, institutional performance, and credible cross-class contact improve; aggregate divergence does not imply uniform distrust within either group.

related_sources.claim: OECD Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions 2026 provides a complementary public-institution and policy-performance trust lens.
WEF Global Risks Report 2026 provides complementary elite-perception analysis of polarization, misinformation, and cooperation risks.

boundary: This record adds a cross-cultural trust, insularity, optimism, class-divergence, and social-media-brokering route. It uses published aggregate survey results and report synthesis, not raw respondent-level records, reweighted microdata, causal attitude models, individual political histories, or proof that trust brokering resolves polarization.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Edelman Trust Barometer 2026 materials were reviewed for the 28-country survey frame, insular mindset, next-generation optimism, influencer trust, and income-based trust-gap findings.
